PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 152 — Lesson 176: Dermatologic, Eye, ENT & Oral Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate lesion morphology, distribution, time course, systemic findings, visual and hearing function, airway risk, medications, exposures, and life-stage context to distinguish common outpatient conditions from skin-, eye-, hearing-, and airway-threatening disease.

Learning Objectives

  • Describe skin findings precisely enough to build a morphology-based differential rather than relying on vague labels.
  • Recognize necrotizing infection, severe cutaneous drug reaction, meningococcemia-pattern illness, anaphylaxis, rapidly progressive blistering disease, and other dermatologic emergencies.
  • Differentiate cellulitis from abscess and common mimics, and identify when drainage or surgical source control is essential.
  • Recognize acute angle-closure glaucoma, infectious keratitis, orbital cellulitis, retinal detachment, retinal vascular occlusion, and chemical eye injury.
  • Apply evidence-based reasoning to sore throat, otitis, sinus symptoms, hearing loss, deep-neck infection, and oral lesions.
  • Use medication safety, infection prevention, biopsy or referral pathways, and explicit result ownership to complete care.

Part 1 — The SURFACE Framework

Skin, eyes, ears, nose, throat, and mouth are visible, but visibility does not guarantee diagnostic simplicity. A red eye can be benign conjunctivitis or a vision-threatening emergency. A red leg can be cellulitis, venous disease, dermatitis, DVT, gout, or necrotizing infection. A sore throat can be viral, streptococcal, abscess-forming, or an airway emergency.

  • S — Stabilize and screen threats: airway, breathing, circulation, anaphylaxis, sepsis, vision loss, severe pain, and rapidly progressive disease.
  • U — Understand onset and exposure: medications, contacts, travel, occupation, trauma, procedures, sun, sexual exposure, immune status, and allergens.
  • R — Record morphology and function: lesion type, color, scale, border, distribution, visual acuity, pupils, hearing, voice, swallowing, and oral examination.
  • F — Form the differential: infectious, inflammatory, allergic, autoimmune, neoplastic, vascular, traumatic, toxic, and neurologic mechanisms.
  • A — Ask what test changes care: culture, scraping, dermoscopy, biopsy, fluorescein, pressure measurement, imaging, hearing testing, or microbiologic testing.
  • C — Control cause and complications: source control, medication withdrawal, targeted therapy, eye or airway protection, and prevention.
  • E — Escalate and ensure closure: emergency care, urgent specialty evaluation, pathology ownership, reassessment, and return precautions.

Part 2 — First Decision: Is There a Threat to Life, Vision, Hearing, or Tissue?

Emergency findings include stridor, drooling with respiratory distress, tongue or facial swelling, hypotension, widespread skin pain or detachment, mucosal erosions after a new medication, rapidly spreading erythema with severe pain, crepitus, purpura with toxicity, sudden visual loss, painful red eye with reduced acuity, orbital signs, chemical ocular exposure, or sudden neurologic hearing loss.

Do not begin with a perfect dermatologic label when physiology is failing. Stabilize, stop suspected harmful exposure, protect the eye or airway, and activate emergency or specialist resources.

Part 3 — Describe Before You Diagnose

Document primary lesions: macule, patch, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal, or cyst. Add secondary change: scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, fissure, excoriation, lichenification, scar, or atrophy. Record color, blanching, tenderness, warmth, fluctuance, induration, border, and surface.

Distribution adds diagnostic power: localized or generalized, flexural or extensor, acral, dermatomal, photo-distributed, intertriginous, follicular, mucosal, palmar or plantar, symmetric, or exposed-area. Photographs—with consent and secure handling—can document evolution.

Part 4 — History That Changes the Skin Differential

Ask about onset, progression, pain vs itch, fever, mucosal symptoms, new medicines in the preceding weeks, recent infection, sick contacts, travel, animals, occupational or chemical exposure, sun, immune suppression, pregnancy, sexual exposure, and household symptoms.

A complete medication history includes antibiotics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, NSAIDs, immune therapies, over-the-counter agents, and supplements. “No new medicines” may conceal a recent dose increase, intermittent drug, or re-exposure.

Part 5 — Cellulitis vs Its Mimics

Cellulitis is a spreading bacterial infection of dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually unilateral, warm, tender, and poorly demarcated. Bilateral symmetric lower-leg redness without systemic illness should prompt reconsideration: venous stasis dermatitis, edema, contact dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, or another inflammatory process may be more likely.

Assess portal of entry, edema, tinea pedis, wound, lymphedema, immune status, systemic findings, and prior microbiology. Marking a border and arranging early reassessment can clarify trajectory. Failure to improve should trigger diagnostic reassessment rather than automatic antibiotic stacking.

Part 6 — Abscess: Source Control Matters

Fluctuance, focal tenderness, purulent drainage, or a localized collection suggests abscess. Incision and drainage is often the central treatment; antibiotics do not reliably sterilize an undrained collection.

Consider imaging when the examination is uncertain or the collection is deep. Culture is especially helpful with severe infection, recurrent disease, immune compromise, treatment failure, or unusual exposure. Facial, hand, perirectal, genital, deep, or rapidly progressive infections may require specialty care.

Part 7 — Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection

Severe pain out of proportion, rapid progression, edema beyond visible erythema, bullae, dusky color, anesthesia, crepitus, systemic toxicity, or shock suggests necrotizing infection. Early skin findings can appear modest.

This is a surgical emergency. Do not delay surgical consultation for normal early laboratory values, lack of gas on plain films, or temporary improvement after analgesia. Resuscitation, broad antimicrobial therapy, and urgent operative source control are required.

Part 8 — Impetigo, Ecthyma, and Superficial Infection

Impetigo commonly produces honey-colored crusted lesions; bullous forms occur with toxin-producing organisms. Ecthyma extends more deeply and ulcerates. Limited disease may be treated topically, while extensive disease or outbreak context can require systemic therapy.

Consider culture with recurrent, widespread, treatment-resistant, or outbreak-associated disease. Hygiene, covering draining lesions, and avoiding shared personal items reduce transmission.

Part 9 — Folliculitis and Hidradenitis Suppurativa

Folliculitis centers on hair follicles and may follow occlusion, shaving, pools, or infection. Recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, and scarring in axillae, groin, inframammary, or gluteal areas suggest hidradenitis suppurativa rather than simple recurrent boils.

HS is chronic inflammatory disease, not poor hygiene. Address pain, tobacco exposure, metabolic comorbidity, weight-neutral counseling, drainage when acutely needed, scarring, mental health, and early dermatology-directed disease control.

Part 10 — Herpes Zoster

Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a unilateral dermatomal distribution with neuropathic pain suggest zoster. Antiviral benefit is greatest when treatment begins early, but new lesions, severe disease, immune compromise, or high-risk location can still influence treatment after the usual window.

Ophthalmic distribution, eye symptoms, ear involvement with facial weakness, disseminated lesions, neurologic findings, pregnancy exposure, or immune compromise changes urgency. Keep lesions covered and counsel regarding exposure to susceptible people.

Part 11 — Tinea, Candidiasis, and Scabies

Dermatophyte disease often has an advancing scaly border and may involve skin, scalp, feet, groin, or nails. Topical corticosteroids can obscure morphology and worsen fungal disease. KOH preparation or culture can clarify uncertain or treatment-resistant cases.

Scabies causes intense nocturnal itch, burrows, and involvement of finger webs, wrists, waist, genitals, or other characteristic sites; infants and immunocompromised patients can differ. Treat close contacts and the environment as recommended. Recurrent candidiasis may signal diabetes, medications, moisture, or immune dysfunction.

Part 12 — Atopic and Contact Dermatitis

Atopic dermatitis is a chronic pruritic barrier disorder with age-dependent distribution. Treatment combines emollients, trigger reduction, appropriately potent anti-inflammatory therapy, infection recognition, and itch-scratch interruption.

Contact dermatitis may be irritant or allergic. Distribution often reflects exposure. Eyelids, hands, occupational sites, and sharply patterned lesions provide clues. Patch testing can identify delayed hypersensitivity when avoidance is unclear. Avoid long courses of high-potency corticosteroids on thin or occluded skin.

Part 13 — Psoriasis

Psoriasis often causes well-demarcated plaques with scale on extensor surfaces, scalp, umbilicus, or gluteal cleft; inverse and pustular patterns differ. Examine nails and ask about joint pain, morning stiffness, dactylitis, heel pain, and inflammatory back symptoms.

Severe generalized pustular or erythrodermic disease can destabilize temperature, fluid, and infection risk and requires urgent specialty care. Management includes cardiovascular and metabolic risk, depression, medication triggers, and psoriatic arthritis recognition.

Part 14 — Acne and Rosacea

Comedones distinguish acne from many mimics. Grade inflammatory burden, nodules, scarring, pigment change, menstrual or androgen clues, and psychosocial impact. Treatment must account for pregnancy potential, irritation, antibiotic stewardship, and the delayed time to improvement.

Rosacea causes central facial erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, inflammatory lesions, and sometimes ocular symptoms without comedones. Eye pain, photophobia, or visual change requires ocular evaluation rather than skin treatment alone.

Part 15 — Urticaria, Angioedema, and Anaphylaxis

Urticaria consists of transient pruritic wheals that typically move and resolve within 24 hours at each site. Lesions persisting in one location, bruising, pain, or systemic findings suggest another process such as urticarial vasculitis.

Angioedema with tongue, laryngeal, or airway involvement can be life-threatening. Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis involving rapid multisystem or airway/circulatory compromise. Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line; antihistamines do not replace it. Observe, prescribe an emergency plan when appropriate, and identify triggers or medication mechanisms.

Part 16 — Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

Skin pain, targetoid or dusky lesions, blistering, epidermal detachment, fever, and mucosal erosions after medication exposure raise concern for Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Facial edema, diffuse eruption, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and internal-organ injury can suggest DRESS.

Stop suspected culprit medicines and arrange emergency hospital-based dermatology and supportive care. Do not rechallenge casually. Clearly document the drug, phenotype, timing, and severity rather than using the nonspecific label “rash allergy.”

Part 17 — Purpura and Nonblanching Rash

Petechiae and purpura do not blanch. Differential diagnosis includes thrombocytopenia, vasculitis, infection, embolic disease, trauma, and coagulation disorders. A toxic patient with rapidly spreading purpura, fever, hypotension, or altered mental status needs emergency sepsis evaluation.

Palpable purpura can suggest small-vessel vasculitis. Assess kidney, GI, joint, pulmonary, and neurologic involvement; medication and infection triggers; CBC; urinalysis; renal function; and need for biopsy or specialty care.

Part 18 — Blistering Disease

Vesicles and bullae can arise from infection, contact reactions, burns, autoimmune disease, edema, friction, or medication. Tense bullae suggest a deeper split; fragile bullae and erosions suggest a superficial split, but clinical overlap exists.

Widespread blistering, mucosal disease, eye involvement, skin pain, fever, or immune compromise demands urgent dermatology evaluation. Biopsy technique and site matter; coordinate rather than sampling an eroded center indiscriminately.

Part 19 — Skin Cancer Recognition

Use ABCDE for melanoma suspicion: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter as one clue, and evolution. The “ugly duckling” lesion that differs from the patient's others and any new or changing lesion deserve attention. Melanoma can occur in sun-protected, acral, nail, mucosal, and darker skin sites.

Basal cell carcinoma often appears pearly, ulcerated, or nonhealing; squamous cell carcinoma may be scaly, keratotic, tender, or ulcerated. Do not destroy a diagnostically uncertain lesion before obtaining appropriate tissue. Pathology ownership is part of the procedure.

Part 20 — Pressure Injury and Chronic Wounds

Chronic wounds require assessment of pressure, perfusion, neuropathy, edema, infection, nutrition, glucose, smoking, mobility, and the patient's capacity for offloading and dressing care. Surface size alone does not reveal undermining, depth, or ischemia.

Urgent concerns include spreading infection, systemic illness, exposed bone, gas, necrosis, severe ischemic pain, or new neurovascular compromise. Antibiotics do not heal an unoffloaded pressure wound or restore arterial flow.

Part 21 — Eye Assessment Starts With Visual Acuity

For almost every eye complaint, record visual acuity in each eye with correction if available. Assess pupils, extraocular movements, visual fields, external structures, conjunctiva, cornea, anterior chamber clues, and fluorescein staining when appropriate.

Reduced acuity, severe pain, photophobia, abnormal pupil, corneal opacity, proptosis, restricted eye movements, or sudden visual field loss moves the case beyond uncomplicated conjunctivitis.

Part 22 — Conjunctivitis Is Not Every Red Eye

Viral conjunctivitis often has watery discharge and contagious exposure; bacterial disease more often has purulent discharge; allergic disease is usually bilateral and intensely itchy. Clinical overlap is substantial, and many cases are self-limited.

Pain, photophobia, reduced vision, contact-lens use, corneal finding, trauma, chemical exposure, or ciliary flush suggests keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma, or another serious process. Avoid topical anesthetic prescriptions and empiric ocular steroids without ophthalmic guidance.

Part 23 — Infectious Keratitis

Contact-lens use, trauma, corneal surgery, ocular-surface disease, or immune suppression increase risk. Pain, photophobia, reduced acuity, focal corneal opacity, and fluorescein uptake are concerning.

Bacterial keratitis can progress rapidly and requires same-day ophthalmologic evaluation and targeted therapy. Remove contact lenses, retain lens or case for culture if directed, and do not patch a suspected infected cornea.

Part 24 — Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma and Uveitis

Acute angle closure may cause severe eye pain, headache, nausea, halos, reduced vision, a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, and a hazy cornea. It is an emergency because sustained pressure can permanently damage vision.

Anterior uveitis can produce deep pain, consensual photophobia, reduced vision, and ciliary flush. Both require urgent ophthalmologic care; labeling them conjunctivitis delays vision-saving treatment.

Part 25 — Chemical Eye Injury

Chemical exposure requires immediate copious irrigation before a lengthy history or visual-acuity testing. Remove contaminated materials and contact lenses when possible, check ocular surface pH according to protocol, continue irrigation until neutral, then complete examination and urgent ophthalmology coordination.

Alkali injury can penetrate rapidly. Do not delay irrigation while identifying the exact product or locating a specialist.

Part 26 — Flashes, Floaters, and Retinal Detachment

New flashes, a sudden increase in floaters, a curtain or shadow, peripheral field loss, or decreased vision can indicate a retinal tear or detachment. Risk increases with high myopia, trauma, prior ocular surgery, or prior detachment.

These symptoms require prompt dilated retinal evaluation. A normal nondilated primary-care examination cannot reliably exclude a peripheral tear.

Part 27 — Sudden Painless Vision Loss

Retinal artery occlusion produces sudden painless monocular vision loss and is treated as an ocular and vascular emergency. Retinal vein occlusion, vitreous hemorrhage, ischemic optic neuropathy, and retinal detachment are other causes.

Establish exact onset, check neurologic symptoms, and activate emergency ophthalmologic and stroke pathways as appropriate. Do not schedule routine optometry follow-up for abrupt major visual loss.

Part 28 — Preseptal vs Orbital Cellulitis

Preseptal cellulitis affects tissues anterior to the orbital septum and may cause eyelid swelling without painful restricted eye movement, proptosis, or visual impairment. Orbital cellulitis can cause pain with eye movement, ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, reduced vision, afferent pupillary abnormality, fever, or severe illness.

Suspected orbital disease requires emergency imaging, IV antimicrobial therapy, and ophthalmology or ENT collaboration because vision loss, abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and intracranial spread can occur.

Part 29 — Otitis Externa and Acute Otitis Media

Otitis externa often causes canal tenderness, tragal or pinna pain, edema, and debris. Severe deep pain, granulation, cranial neuropathy, diabetes, or immune compromise raises concern for invasive external otitis.

Acute otitis media requires middle-ear findings such as bulging tympanic membrane or new otorrhea not from otitis externa—not redness alone. Age, severity, laterality, follow-up reliability, and current guidance determine observation vs antibiotics.

Part 30 — Mastoiditis and Ear Complications

Postauricular erythema, swelling, tenderness, protrusion of the pinna, persistent fever, or toxic appearance after otitis suggests mastoiditis. Facial weakness, vertigo, severe headache, or neurologic findings indicate complicated disease.

These findings require urgent imaging and ENT or hospital evaluation rather than another routine oral antibiotic course.

Part 31 — Sudden Hearing Loss

Differentiate conductive from sensorineural loss using history, otoscopy, and bedside tuning-fork tests when available. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss—often unilateral and noticed on awakening—may be mistaken for ear congestion despite a normal canal and tympanic membrane.

This is an otologic urgency requiring prompt audiologic confirmation and ENT-directed treatment. Do not delay while repeatedly treating presumed eustachian tube dysfunction.

Part 32 — Rhinosinusitis and Antibiotic Stewardship

Most acute sinus symptoms are viral. Bacterial likelihood increases with persistent symptoms without improvement, severe onset with high fever and purulent discharge or facial pain, or worsening after initial improvement. Purulent color alone does not prove bacterial infection.

Assess orbital symptoms, severe frontal headache, swelling, neurologic findings, immune compromise, and toxic appearance for complications. Treatment should match allergy history, local guidance, recent antibiotics, and follow-up—not patient pressure alone.

Part 33 — Pharyngitis

Cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, oral ulcers, and conjunctivitis strongly support a viral cause. When viral features are absent, clinical examination alone cannot reliably distinguish group A streptococcal pharyngitis; use recommended testing.

CDC guidance recommends confirmatory culture after a negative rapid antigen test in symptomatic children age three and older, while routine backup culture is usually unnecessary in adults. Treat confirmed group A strep and avoid antibiotics for viral illness or asymptomatic carriage in most circumstances.

Part 34 — Deep-Neck and Airway Threats

Drooling, stridor, tripod positioning, muffled voice, trismus, unilateral swelling, uvular deviation, neck stiffness or swelling, inability to swallow secretions, respiratory distress, or toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal infection, Ludwig angina, or another deep-space process.

Do not agitate a patient with a potentially unstable airway or force an examination that could worsen obstruction. Activate emergency airway, imaging, drainage, and ENT resources in a controlled setting.

Part 35 — Oral Lesions and Oral Cancer

Assess dental disease, trauma, aphthous ulcers, candidiasis, herpes, immune status, tobacco, alcohol, betel nut, HPV exposure, medication, and duration. An ulcer, erythroplakia, leukoplakia, mass, unexplained bleeding, unilateral pain, or neck node persisting beyond expected healing requires dental, ENT, or oral-surgery evaluation and often biopsy.

Oral candidiasis may reflect inhaled corticosteroid technique, antibiotics, dentures, diabetes, or immune compromise. Treat the lesion while addressing the cause.

Part 36 — Life-Stage Modifiers

Children: rapidly evolving airway disease, nonblanching rash, dehydration, orbital complications, mastoiditis, abuse-related injury, and weight-based medication safety matter. Pregnancy: drug selection, melasma and benign changes, cholestatic itch, hypertensive visual symptoms, and pregnancy-specific dermatoses alter care. Older adults: zoster, skin cancer, bullous disease, hearing loss, glaucoma, medication effects, and atypical infection are more common.

Skin findings can look different across pigmentation. Erythema may appear violaceous, gray, dark brown, or subtle; rely on warmth, edema, scale, texture, blanching, tenderness, and comparison—not redness alone.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 1: Necrotizing Infection

A patient with diabetes has rapidly worsening leg pain far greater than visible erythema, tense edema, a dusky bulla, tachycardia, and hypotension.

Reasoning: Pain out of proportion, rapid progression, bullae, and shock suggest necrotizing soft-tissue infection. Emergency surgical consultation, resuscitation, and broad antimicrobial therapy must not wait for outpatient imaging.

Part 38 — Board-Style Case 2: Severe Drug Reaction

Two weeks after starting a high-risk medication, a patient develops fever, skin pain, dusky targetoid lesions, oral erosions, and blistering.

Reasoning: Mucosal disease and painful blistering after a new drug suggest SJS/TEN. Stop suspected drugs and arrange emergency hospital-based dermatology and supportive care.

Part 39 — Board-Style Case 3: Painful Red Eye

A contact-lens wearer has severe unilateral eye pain, photophobia, reduced visual acuity, and a focal corneal opacity.

Reasoning: This pattern suggests infectious keratitis rather than uncomplicated conjunctivitis. Same-day ophthalmology evaluation is required to prevent corneal destruction and vision loss.

Part 40 — Board-Style Case 4: Retinal Threat

A highly myopic patient reports sudden new flashes, many floaters, and a curtain descending across peripheral vision.

Reasoning: These are classic retinal tear or detachment warnings requiring prompt dilated retinal examination. Routine follow-up is unsafe.

Part 41 — Board-Style Case 5: Airway Risk

A patient has rapidly progressive submandibular swelling, fever, muffled voice, drooling, and difficulty handling secretions after a dental infection.

Reasoning: Deep-space infection such as Ludwig angina can obstruct the airway. Emergency airway and ENT or surgical management takes priority over routine oral antibiotics.

Part 42 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: Bilateral red legs equal bilateral cellulitis. Correction: stasis and inflammatory mimics are often more likely; assess asymmetry, warmth, tenderness, edema, and systemic findings.
  • Trap: Antibiotics cure every abscess. Correction: drainage is often the essential source control.
  • Trap: Every red eye is conjunctivitis. Correction: pain, photophobia, reduced acuity, contact lenses, corneal change, or abnormal pupil requires urgent evaluation.
  • Trap: Diameter below 6 mm excludes melanoma. Correction: evolution and ugly-duckling change matter at any size.
  • Trap: Colored nasal discharge proves bacterial sinusitis. Correction: duration, severity, and double worsening are more useful.
  • Trap: Exudative throat always means strep. Correction: viral and other infections overlap; test in the correct clinical setting.

Part 43 — Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Stabilize: identify airway compromise, anaphylaxis, sepsis, severe drug reaction, tissue necrosis, and acute sensory loss.
  2. Describe: morphology, distribution, onset, exposure, visual acuity, pupils, hearing, voice, swallowing, and oral findings.
  3. Name cannot-miss alternatives: necrotizing infection, SJS/TEN, invasive infection, glaucoma, keratitis, orbital disease, retinal event, or deep-neck infection.
  4. Test selectively: culture, scraping, biopsy, fluorescein, pressure, imaging, audiology, or microbiology must answer a defined question.
  5. Treat mechanism and source: remove culprit, drain collection, use targeted therapy, protect eye or airway, and address exposure.
  6. Escalate appropriately: emergency, same-day specialty, expedited biopsy, or structured outpatient care.
  7. Close the loop: own pathology and cultures, verify response, educate on prevention, and document return precautions.

High-Yield Summary

  • Morphology plus distribution and time course is more diagnostic than the word “rash.”
  • Pain out of proportion and rapid progression suggest necrotizing infection even before dramatic skin change.
  • Skin pain, mucosal erosions, and blistering after a medication suggest severe cutaneous drug reaction.
  • Visual acuity is a vital sign of the eye; pain, photophobia, reduced vision, corneal change, or abnormal pupil is not routine conjunctivitis.
  • New flashes, floaters, curtain, or sudden painless visual loss requires urgent retinal or stroke-related evaluation.
  • Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an urgency despite a normal otoscopic examination.
  • Use GAS testing appropriately and recognize airway or deep-neck warning signs before routine sore-throat management.
  • Every culture, biopsy, pathology result, sensory complaint, and referral requires explicit follow-up ownership.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational. Apply current AAD, AAO, IDSA, CDC, local ophthalmology and ENT pathways, antimicrobial guidance, and patient-specific emergency protocols in practice.
